item.title: Demolition of Dunn Solar Telescope to Start Soon
item.description:
Demolition of the Dunn Solar Telescope at Sunspot Solar Observatory is slated to begin as early as next week and will proceed through March 2027, Alamogordo Town News has learned.

The Dunn, an iconic feature of the Sacramento Mountains skyline since 1969, used three liquid mercury bearings to ensure smooth rotation of its vertical telescope as it studied how sunspots, flares, and other solar features form. On Jan. 6, one of the two upper bearings leaked about 186 pounds of mercury (about 6 quarts), prompting NSF to close the Dunn.

On Feb. 24, NSF concluded that the Dunn should be demolished given the highly toxic nature of mercury. Thornton Tomasetti, a major engineering firm based in New York, was contracted to analyze and then to remove an estimated nine tons of mercury. On Aug. 27, Thornton Tomasetti reported that while the mercury was removed, decades of small leaks and vapors had likely compromised the telescope’s structure.

While not been formally announced, the National Science Foundation today confirmed that demolition will proceed under a new $9,999,334 contract, with a Sept. 23, 2026–March 23, 2027 period of performance.

This brings the total value of Thornton Tomasetti’s three contracts to $13.7 million, listed first as “SAC PEAK MERCURY STABILITY EFFORT” and twice as “SAC PEAK MERCURY DRAINING EFFORTS.”

Three aspects of the latest contract are unusual.

First, it was awarded as a “draining effort” after NSF confirmed that mercury had been drained. NSF said this description was a mistake.

“Regarding the task order description, we appreciate you bringing this to our attention, as the current description is incorrect,” an NSF spokesperson wrote is response to an ATN inquiry. “The correct task order description is ‘SAC Peak DST Demolition MERCURY REMEDIATION Effort,’ which includes both the ongoing mercury remediation activities and the associated demolition efforts.”

Second, the award amount is $666 below the $10 million threshold of the Federal Truth In Negotiations Act, “a powerful fraud enforcement tool [requiring contractors] to provide full and complete price and cost information when submitting for bids,” as described in a 2024 article in The National Review.

Third, the $3 million mercury removal contract (posted July 10) and this new $10 million demolition contract (posted Sept. 10) were not published on the government’s System for Award Management (SAM.gov) where most purchases are solicited and then announced. ATN found the contract amounts by searching on USASpending.gov, which lists obligations and outlays.

ATN asked why neither was advertised, giving the appearance of a sole-source, unadvertised contract, and asked for a copy of the statement of work.

NSF’s reply did not fully answer the question: “For public information on the contract, please refer to the justification posted on April 30, 2026, on SAM.gov under Notice ID NSF260002, which includes the justification for a sole source contract [the first contract, with a final value of $670,679] and the services required to meet the agency’s needs: https://sam.gov/workspace/contract/opp/570137d5bba64869b2cc4dd13d0280fa/view.”

That announcement was a brief explanation of the mercury remediation contract being sole-source/CUI (Confidential, Unclassified Information). A 2010 Executive order defines CUI as “unclassified information throughout the executive branch that requires safeguarding or dissemination controls [and replaced an] inefficient, confusing patchwork” of regulations.

ATN reported the CUI explanation for the Dunn in a previous story, “Sunspot Telescope leak was small, but dangerous.”

Note: The author, Dave Dooling,  is a veteran science writer and former education officer at Sunspot.

item.title: Tularosa Homecoming Parade to Close Highway 54/70 and Nearby Streets Thursday Afternoon
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — Drivers passing through Tularosa on Thursday, Sept. 17, should plan for delays as the Tularosa Police Department temporarily closes several roads, including a stretch of U.S. Highway 54/70, for the Tularosa Municipal Schools Homecoming Parade.

The parade begins at 1 p.m. Police said Granado Street will close first, at noon, so students at the elementary and middle schools have a clear view of the festivities. Traffic on St. Francis Drive, which carries U.S. Highway 54/70 through town, will begin shutting down at 12:50 p.m. Roads are expected to reopen at about 1:20 p.m.

Affected roads include St. Francis Drive from Alamo Street to Higuera Avenue, Wildcat Turf Road, 8th Street, Bosque Street, and Granado Street to First Street.

Police recommend that motorists use South Bookout Road to Central Avenue to avoid the parade route.

That detour is not open to semi-trucks or oversized loads, however, and the department said no alternate route exists for those vehicles. Commercial drivers traveling St. Francis Drive will have to stop and wait until the parade ends and the highway reopens.

After the parade, officers will direct traffic at the Higuera Avenue signal and will stay in the area until congestion clears and normal traffic flow returns.

The department asked drivers to use caution, follow the directions of traffic control personnel, and watch for pedestrians and parade participants. Police thanked the community for its patience in helping keep the celebration safe for students and families.

item.title: Otero County Commission tables subdivision fee hikes; sheriff reports 40-pound meth seizure
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Otero County Commission on Tuesday, Sept. 15, put off a proposal to raise the county's subdivision and planning fees. Commissioners said the increases could discourage development in a county already struggling to attract builders.

Commissioners voted unanimously to table the resolution until the November meeting. Commissioner Gerald Matherly, who led the opposition, plans to meet privately with planning staff before a revised fee schedule comes back.

Matherly argued that subdividers already pay substantial property taxes once land is divided and developed, and that reviewing their plans is a basic county service. "I'm in Otero County. I'm trying to take care of my people," he said. "It's hard enough to try to get people to do subdivisions and do work around here." He said large subdivision activity is limited mostly to Chaparral and appears to be slowing. He did not object to higher fees for road and easement vacations, which he called "above and beyond" services.

A second commissioner called the proposed increases "pretty drastic." That commissioner pointed to the county's efforts to encourage economic growth, including a joint initiative with Lincoln County, and suggested revisiting fees once development picks up.

County planning staff said the fees have not changed in at least 16 years. Most of the office's workload now comes from claims of exemption, which are simple land splits that fall outside the formal subdivision process. Those filings cost $15, and 38 had been filed this year through August. Staff said rising mapping costs justify raising that fee in particular.

Staff also noted that the Planning Commission is rewriting subdivision regulations last updated in 2013. They said decades of minimal requirements left many properties without adequate surveys, easements or floodplain review, and newer homeowners sometimes find out when monsoon rains flood their homes. The goal is to require enough review to prevent that without making it too expensive for residents to divide small parcels.

The debate turned to how Alamogordo's growth affects county residents. Matherly said development inside city limits has redirected stormwater onto county properties, and argued the county should have a voice in municipal planning. Staff encouraged closer coordination with the city. A commissioner suggested county planning commissioners attend city planning meetings.

Consent agenda and road actions

On its consent agenda, the commission approved:

• a $580,125 Operation Stonegarden grant from the Department of Homeland Security,

• the 2026 tax rates,

• a September budget adjustment,

• two requests for proposals for the Juvenile Justice Advisory Committee,

• a second grant agreement of about $625,899,

• a resolution declaring a property a public nuisance and moving it toward condemnation.

Commissioners also approved a resolution confirming a 60-foot public right-of-way along the Alamogordo Drive and Lonesome Dove corridors. The resolution authorizes a retracement survey to find where those rights-of-way actually lie.

The issue arose from a driveway permit for a solar project on Mesa Verde Ranch land. Staff said newly located records from 1900 and 1904 show the original dedication, but existing roads may have drifted from their recorded locations. The county does not plan to move any roads, and a 2019 settlement between Mesa Verde and a neighboring owner will stand. One other property could be affected, but its owner died in June and the county has not reached his heir.

The commission also appointed viewers for a proposed road vacation on Del Rio Chiquita. The vacation would let a homeowner reach the three-quarter-acre minimum needed for a septic system.

Sheriff's office and dispatch

Sheriff David Black said the White Mountain Drug Task Force wrapped up a long-running operation the day before. One man was arrested and about 20 kilograms, roughly 40 pounds, of methamphetamine was seized. Black said that was about 19 kilos more than investigators expected. The Alamogordo Police Department, several other agencies and the DEA took part, and a press release is expected.

In August, the sheriff's office logged 1,902 calls for service and 90 arrests. Narcotics officers served 12 search warrants and made 38 arrests. They seized about $35,000 in drugs and cash, including fentanyl powder, 133 fentanyl pills and three firearms. Deputies also launched D.A.R.E. programs at four elementary schools.

Black said four cadets are in the academy in Hobbs and two positions remain open. Three of 12 new patrol units have arrived and are being outfitted with striping and radios. Eddy County also donated 10 used vehicles that Black said are in good condition. A commissioner asked the sheriff to remove an abandoned trailer that has sat on the Lollygate Road easement for eight weeks.

The regional dispatch center received 6,744 calls in August, including 1,639 calls to 911, and dispatched 4,316 calls. It has 10 fully trained dispatchers and one in training.

Emergency services and roads

Emergency Services Director Matt Clark said volunteer fire departments answered 351 calls in August, 277 of them medical. Burn restrictions remain in place despite recent rain, because a statewide restriction covering private property would still apply.

Clark said the county's Sept. 11 anniversary parade included a Native Air flyover for the first time. He invited commissioners to a first responder rally on Oct. 2. He also praised the Forest Service and volunteer departments for keeping recent fires small. The county's roads superintendent said crews are preparing Sixteen Springs for chip seal, though dry conditions have slowed work. Crews are also coordinating with the Forest Service to repair a road damaged in last year's fire.

Construction projects

The county's project manager said the first construction package for the new district courthouse is proposed at about $9.5 million, roughly $115,000 under the original estimate. Excavation could begin in October, weather permitting.

Designs for the Chaparral law enforcement facility are moving forward on an expedited schedule. The prefabricated building for the grant-funded animal shelter ships from Pennsylvania Sept. 28. The fairgrounds animal barn roof will be replaced after the fair. One flood mitigation design is complete and another is 90% done.

Staff said a special meeting will be needed before Sept. 30 to approve a Timberon guardrail grant.

Detention center

The detention center's average daily population was 181 in August, and it has eight staff vacancies. The director said placing juvenile detainees remains difficult. The facility is also dealing with boiler, water heater and plumbing problems, much of it in cast-iron lines dating to 1998.

Forest Service

Cecilia Clay, acting supervisor of the Lincoln National Forest, introduced herself and pledged closer cooperation with the county. A Forest Service official said a fire burning in rugged terrain to the south was expected to be contained within days. The forest's last timber sale of the fiscal year was its largest since 2006.

Commissioners criticized an off-road vehicle gathering over Labor Day weekend that drew more than 250 vehicles and left damage and trash behind, much of it from out-of-town visitors. The Forest Service said it now tracks social media posts about such events and requires permits. The sheriff's office helped patrol that weekend. One commissioner urged support for HR 9536, a congressional bill that would limit environmental groups' lawsuits against federal agencies.

Tularosa water and other reports

Commissioners discussed the village of Tularosa's continuing water problems. Its tanks were full as of last week, but the holding pond remains low. The village is borrowing a pump from Cloudcroft, and the ditch corporation is replacing a headgate.

The village plans a reverse-osmosis system to use as a backup, and a commissioner has been asking how its brine could be disposed of safely. Staff pointed the village to $35 million in state grants for brackish water projects. Staff also said the state has not answered the county's request, now four weeks old, to reimburse emergency water hauling.

The commission chair, president-elect of the New Mexico Association of Counties, reported on:

• an interview with a Japanese newspaper,

• an upcoming Business News Magazine feature on Otero County's economic development,

• mental health talks with Lincoln County and the Mescalero Apache Tribe,

• negotiations over Bonita Lake with the city, Lincoln County and the state.

She also said New Mexico's only New World screwworm case, in a Lea County dog, was cleared Aug. 30, though Texas has several cases. Matherly said he resigned from the grazing board and recommended the chair replace him.

County officials said:

• an insurance broker contract and a cooperating agency agreement for the Western Gateway pipeline project will come to the commission in October,

• interviews are underway for a human resources director and a replacement for landfill manager Ralph Murphy,

• nearly all employees now receive paychecks by direct deposit,

• the county's move away from paper checks to vendors has been slowed by software errors.

Commissioners also discussed a landowner's offer to donate land and a large flagpole at a highway junction, and asked staff for draft agreement language covering maintenance. They asked about the status of a plaque dedicating the emergency services building to Matt Starr.

The commission issued three proclamations. It declared September Suicide Prevention Awareness Month and encouraged residents to take the state's free ABC suicide intervention training. It marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. It also named Sept. 22 Sgt. Willie Estrada Day, honoring the Alamogordo native killed in action in Korea on that date in 1952. Estrada is Otero County's only recipient of the Distinguished Service Cross.

item.title: In Memory of Sadie Jo Stogden
item.description:
Sadie Jo Stogden was a devoted wife, loving mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, sister, aunt, beloved Nina and friend. She lived a life rooted in faith, family, service, and an unwavering desire to care for others.

Sadie is now reunited in eternal life with her beloved husband, Robert Gomez Stogden; her mother, Bessie Gonzales; her father, Lazaro Gonzales; her brothers, Rudy Gonzales, George Gonzales, and Albert Gonzales; her sister-in-law, Gloria Gonzales; and her grandsons, Lawrence "Lencho" Arriola and James Arriola.
She leaves behind a beautiful family who will forever carry her love and memory. She is survived by her son, Alfonso Stogden Sr., and his wife, Lidia Stogden; her daughter, Melissa Arriola, and her husband, Lawrence Arriola; her four grandchildren, Alfonso Stogden Jr., Rebecca Stogden, Robert Arriola, and Jesse Arriola, and nine great-grandchildren; her brothers, Edward Gonzales and Charles Gonzales, and his wife, Patricia Gonzales, along with many extended family members and loved ones whose lives she touched.

Sadie was a devoted Catholic and longtime member of Immaculate Conception Catholic Church. Her faith was an important part of her life. She generously gave many years of her time to the church, especially enjoying the annual fiesta and faithfully attending Saturday evening Mass.

Sadie dedicated much of her life to working with and caring for children. She retired from the Los Angeles Unified School District, where her passion for helping young people was evident throughout her career. She later spent more than 25 years at the Zia Therapy Center, a place that brought her great joy and allowed her to continue doing what she loved most-helping and caring for others.
Sadie had a giving heart and a natural desire to help those around her. Whether through her faith, her work, her family, or simple acts of kindness, she made people feel cared for and loved.
Above all, Sadie’s greatest love was her family. Her strength, compassion, faith, and generous spirit will continue to live on through the generations she leaves behind.

Sadie leaves a beautiful legacy of faith and love-not only within her family, but in the hearts of everyone blessed enough to have crossed her path. She will be deeply missed, forever loved, and never forgotten.

Services will be held Thursday, September 17th at Immaculate Conception Catholic Church beginning at 9:00 am with a viewing, followed by the Rosary at 9:30, Mass of Christian Burial at 10:30 and graveside at Immaculate Conception Catholic Cemetery at 11:45. A potluck luncheon will be held the ICCC Hall from 12:00 pm till 4:00 pm.

item.title: Save the Date: Alamogordo to Welcome Home Honor Flight Veteran September 26th at VFW Post 7686
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, NM — Mark your calendars for Saturday, September 26, 2026, at 7:00 PM, when Alamogordo will once again line up to welcome home one of its own. A local veteran is returning from his Honor Flight trip to Washington, D.C., and the community is invited to give him the reception he has earned at VFW Post 7686, 700 Hwy 70 W.

The event is hosted by the U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, with support from Rio Grande Honor Flight and the Patriot Guard Riders. This fall's homecoming moves to the VFW post on Highway 70, a new setting for a tradition that has grown in recent years. Contact the post at 575-437-0770 for details.

A Trip of a Lifetime

Honor Flight trips give veterans the chance to see the memorials built in their honor. On past flights, local veterans have visited Arlington and the Vietnam and Korean War memorials. Rio Grande Honor Flight provides these trips free to veterans, funded by community donations and volunteers. Organizers describe the journey as one that brings closure and healing, along with the welcome home these heroes deserve.

For many Vietnam-era veterans, that last part matters most. At a 2022 homecoming, organizers shared one veteran's reflection that having people cheer and show pride in him healed wounds others could not imagine.

A Growing Alamogordo Tradition

The Trinity Chapter has made these homecomings a local fixture. Chartered in 2018, the chapter has joined the Patriot Guard Riders in welcoming several groups of Honor Flight veterans, turning the returns into yearly celebrations of gratitude in Alamogordo. Details of this honoree is still pending and will be featured in an upcoming story. 

The turnout has been strong. In September 2024, three Vietnam-era veterans returning on Honor Flight #18 were greeted at the Otero County Fairgrounds by a large, enthusiastic crowd. In April 2025, residents gathered on New York Avenue to honor retired Air Force Lt. Col. Gloria Fernandez and retired Senior Master Sgt. Thomas McKean. Most recently, on April 25, 2026, the city welcomed Chris Hall and Lucio Vazquez, both Vietnam-era veterans, with a flag-line escort from the Trinity Chapter and Patriot Guard Riders, backed by State Police, Alamogordo Police, and Otero County Sheriff's Office support.

How You Can Help

Organizers ask residents to arrive early, bring American flags and handmade signs, and wear red, white, and blue. The veteran's arrival is typically escorted by motorcycle riders and local law enforcement, and a crowd waiting for him is the best part of the homecoming.

VFW Post 7686 continues its year of service to local veterans after participating in a 9/11 remembrance car show earlier this month. As Post Commander Ryan "Check" Nowaczck said in May, "Your presence matters." On September 26th, it will.

Event Details

What: Welcome Home for Our Hero

When: Saturday, September 26, 2026, 7:00 PM

Where: VFW Post 7686, 700 Hwy 70 W, Alamogordo

Hosted by: U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter

Info: riograndehonorflight.org

item.title: Bonito Lake: 9/22 City of Alamogordo Commission Meeting, Agenda Item #8

An update to the 8/30 article by Otero County Botanicals. Pictured is a still from the 8/25 meeting video.
https://oteronativeplants.substack.com/p/bonito-lake-why-suddenly-fence-it

I encourage all interested parties, especially the entities named in the agenda item (link), below, to attend the meeting, and make public comment.
• Holloman AFB
• New Mexico Department of Wildlife
• State of New Mexico
• Lincoln County
• Village of Ruidoso
• City of Ruidoso Downs

It’s my desire to see the commission examine all aspects of Bonito Lake, and make up a comprehensive plan on how to move forward, even if creating that plan takes multiple meetings. There’s no need, or rush, to devalue the lake’s recreational amenities and value, and break precedent and plans already in place. And while the recommendation for the city to examine options with stakeholders, is great, and is already started, since the 9/1 public forum, there’s great cause for hesitation and skepticism in a 6 month timeframe with minimal requirements/expectations, and with staff who still isn’t showing the commission all the appropriate documents and information about the item.

On 8/25, when the commission tabled the item, it asked for the following information. It’s thus far not listed in the upcoming agenda.
• Annual attendance
• A history of area lawsuits

During the 8/25 meeting, and again for the 9/22 meeting, why weren’t the following items included?
• The 2024-2028 Open Gate Agreement with NMDOW. The 1st staff recommendation was to cancel the agreement. Not disclosed was the refund amount, if cancelled, that I estimate to be $22k. Under the contract’s “Notice of Possible Municipal Action” clause, NMDOW should have been informed ahead of time of both the 8/25 and 9/25 meetings, otherwise it’s a “material breach of this Agreement.”
• The 2024 Parks & Recreation Master Plan. “Bonito Lake is a special facility owned by the City. While the priority is to replace the existing road, there is a great need to improve the campgrounds and associated facilities so that Bonito Lake can be reopened to the public for day use, overnight camping, hiking, and fishing.”
• The “$250,000 State appropriation” is finally mentioned for 9/22. What wasn’t mentioned is that it was the (2025) 1st of “five (5) recommended capital outlay projects for Fiscal Years 2027-2031… ,“ out of a list of 67 possible projects.

Regarding the Utilities Department work, including fencing the dam/spillway, debris mitigation, retention basins (sediment ponds), Rodamaker Canyon, etc. I’ve mentioned that this is separate from recreation, meaning the Parks & Recreation Department, the Open Gate Agreement with NMDOW, and should not be tied/jumbled together. It’s both important and urgent to get resolved, and relates to water rates, which just might have to increase for this. For clarification, the lake should never have to be dredged again, and the duck pond (last stopgap) is half full, with no road down into it to pump it.

Regarding the priorities, there is no 1st priority for drinking water, 2nd priority for recreation, unless the commission make that precedent. It’s always been both, and more. “To manage and preserve Alamogordo’s most valuable source of water supply. To provide the public a clean, safe recreational site in which they can picnic, camp or fish, and to maintain the Bonito Lake Campgrounds, the dam and the Bonito pipeline from the lake to Three Rivers. In addition, to plan and implement Resource Conservation and Development projects.“

NMDOW Agreement Questions:
• Have they been contacted about the “wildlife habitat incentives” in the agreement?
• The Blue Hole / Apple Orchard Campground, which is not on the shoreline, is it exempt from the agreement, and thus would be able to charge fees for parking, camping, etc. ?

Explore ways to make recreation more profitable:
• (10/8-11) Visit Grindstone Lake in Ruidoso to see the Xterra World Championship (fall finales 2026-2028, plus Spring qualifiers). Grindstone lake also charges for parking, boat permits, camping, Wibit (floating inflatable water park). Also their Disc Golf, located outside, is free. Used as movie backdrops.
• The forest service’s Schoolhouse Picnic Area (link), just down the road, charges $5/day (an unattended money drop), and has signs saying “no potable water,” and “pack out your trash.” Fees for day use, and dispersed/primitive camping, would help fund renovations.
• The most requested features in the 2022 survey were camping, fishing, hiking and picnicking. Monetize these, and centralize/reduce staff. Hold special events. Use the area to advertise Alamogordo attractions. Compare to amenities at similar lakes: Inn of the Mountain Gods, Silver Lake, Grindstone Lake, Alto Lake, and also to South Fork Campground.

Regarding Recommendation 3 “…examine possible long-term options for the future of the lake in concert with (entities)… 6 months… ,“ what are desired outcomes? What if nobody else, the State, Lincoln County, Ruidoso, Ruidoso Downs and other stakeholders, can’t or won’t help fund renovations at our lake? Are we then going to revisit fencing off the entire lake. Maybe keep the lake open for fishing, but still not remediate the campgrounds. How about the cost to demolish all the campground facilities, like bathrooms, that look brand new on the outside, but need a little work on the inside.

item.title: Commission to Decide Whether Al Hernandez Complaint Moves Forward, as Two-to-One "No Cause" Finding Exposes Limits of Self-Policing per Weak Charter
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Next Tuesday, the Alamogordo City Commission will vote on whether to pursue a Code of Conduct complaint against one of its own members, Commissioner Alfonso "Al" Hernandez.

The item is No. 10 on the September 22 agenda, submitted by City Manager Robert Stockwell. The complaint was reviewed by a three-member Preliminary Review Committee made up of fellow commissioners. According to the agenda report, two of the three found "No Cause" on all four counts, and the third found "Cause" on all four. Because of that split, the city code requires the full Commission to decide whether the complaint goes any further. Hernandez himself cannot vote.

The threshold is steep. The motion needs five affirmative votes. If it falls short, the agenda report states that "no further action on the complaint may be taken." If it gets five votes, the complaint will be scheduled for a later meeting where its merits will be heard. City staff stress that Tuesday's vote is not about whether the allegations are true, only whether they will be examined at all.

The airport board exchange

The complaint arrives amid public attention on a video clip from a public meeting with the city's airport board. In the clip, Hernandez appears to call the leader of the city employees' union "stupid" and says she is causing problems for the city. The clip has circulated online: https://youtube.com/shorts/THi1Cm40-Rw?is=0sGgMTCJNfPMykxb

A related public records request, No. 26-1438, is on file with the city through its NextRequest portal: https://cityofalamogordonm.nextrequest.com/requests/26-1438.

The city's duty to its workforce

Whatever the Commission decides, the episode raises a basic question: who protects city employees when the person they are dealing with is an elected official?

Employers generally must maintain a workplace free of harassment and retaliation. Union leaders also have legal protections when they advocate for members. When a commissioner publicly disparages an employee representative in an official meeting, the city carries the legal and financial exposure, not the commissioner personally. Local outlet 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News has reported more than $1 million in taxpayer-funded settlements tied to alleged oversteps, including issues involving former Commissioner Al Hernandez and other commissioners. This is not the first complaint against Al Hernandez nor other commissioners to include Josh Rardin via a public records request internal investigations have occurred by outside legal counsel in the past and have found a mixed bag of infractions but little action to sanction fellow commissioners by a commission unwilling to hold fellow members accountable to protecting employees from political pressure and harassment. 

In 2023 an outside investigator found credible allegations that commissioners interfered in daily operations and put staff "in sometimes untenable positions." In 2025 the same outside investigator found the city manager recruitment tainted, with a commissioner's comments creating discrimination exposure for the city. Both problems were identified by outside counsel, not by the commission's own review process as outlined by a weak charter with little regard to accountability and in need of updating. 

Critics say this structure has several built-in weaknesses. There is no independent investigator or outside hearing officer. The five-vote supermajority means a minority of commissioners can end a complaint without any public review of the evidence. And the employee who is the subject of the remarks has no formal role in the decision.

The rules themselves are also muddled. Last year, commissioners identified two separate code-of-conduct ordinances, one passed in 2014 and another in 2022, that overlap and contain inconsistent language, particularly regarding complaint procedures and remedies. At the time, commissioners asked staff to either repeal one ordinance or merge the two into a single, clearer policy. The topic was once again in discussion in 2025. https://citizenportal.ai/articles/6128439/new-mexico/otero-county/alamogordo/commission-asks-staff-to-reconcile-two-city-codes-of-conduct-and-review-social-media-guidance

Supporters of the current system argue that elected officials answer to voters, not staff, and that a high bar protects commissioners from politically motivated complaints. Residents who want another route have options outside City Hall. The city attorney has previously reminded members of complaint options through the New Mexico Attorney General or State Ethics Commission.

What's next

The Commission meets Tuesday, September 22, 2026. Public comment is open at the start of the meeting. If five commissioners vote yes, the complaint's merits will be taken up at a future meeting. If not, the matter ends there.

Hear Hernandez’s own words…

https://youtube.com/shorts/THi1Cm40-Rw?is=ws0t7JT6J2YFs4aQ

item.title: “Will Never Be Released”: Records Show a Pattern of Commissioner Interference and Harassment Allegations That Alamogordo’s Commission Has Rarely Policed
item.description:
Two outside investigations obtained through public records requests describe a pattern of years of commissioners pressuring city employees over code enforcement, a "tainted" recruitment the investigator warned could be called discriminatory, and a pattern that has coincided with settlements and the departure of two city managers. Next Tuesday, the commission decides whether to examine a new complaint against one of its own.

Earlier this year, during public comments at an Alamogordo City Commission meeting, Commissioner Josh Rardin told former Mayor Susan Payne that two outside investigation reports into commission conduct would never be released. 

Excerpts from both reports are now public. 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News obtained them through persistent public records requests and challenges under the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act. 

Both were written by attorney Clara B. Burns of the law firm Kemp Smith LLP. The first, dated Dec. 22, 2023, examined allegations by former City Manager Brian Cesar. The second, dated July 3, 2025, examined whether the search for a permanent city manager was biased against Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez. Commissioner John Rardin is named in both.

In the first report, Burns found that commissioners had broken the city's own Code of Conduct by going around the city manager to pressure employees.

In the second, she concluded that the recruitment had been compromised and warned that it exposed the city to a discrimination claim.

Both city managers at the center of these reports have since left under settlement agreements.

The reports surface as the commission again faces the question of whether it will hold its own members accountable. 

On Tuesday, Sept. 22, commissioners will vote on whether a Code of Conduct complaint against Commissioner Alfonso "Al" Hernandez can move forward. A panel of his fellow commissioners has already recommended dropping it on a 2–1 vote.

Who complained, and in what role prior?

Brian Cesar, former City Manager. Under the City Charter, the city manager is the city's chief executive officer, responsible for enforcing ordinances and hiring and firing employees. On April 11, 2023, Cesar sent a letter to then-Mayor Payne alleging a continued pattern of commissioners violating the Charter, the city's ordinances and the Code of Conduct. According to the report, the letter said commissioners inserted themselves into daily operations and demanded code violations to benefit themselves, friends, family and business partners, at the risk of his job. The city placed his evaluation on an agenda around the same time. Instead of an evaluation, Cesar negotiated a retirement and settlement agreement that required him to cooperate with an investigation. His written answers, dated Oct. 26, 2023, were signed before a notary.

City employees. Burns interviewed current employees whose identities she kept anonymous "to the extent practical" because of their concerns about retaliation. Their accounts supplied much of the evidence behind the credible findings.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, Acting City Manager. In 2025, Hernandez was not the complainant. The report says she did not request the investigation and was opposed to it, fearing it "would place a target on her back," though she cooperated. Then-Mayor Payne and then-Mayor Pro Tem Sharon McDonald, now mayor, raised concerns about Josh Rardin to the investigator. McDonald said a former city commissioner had reported Rardin's comments to her.

2023: "Very aggressive" with staff

Cesar's central claim was that commissioners with ties to the building industry pressured city staff to bend codes and standards for developers. Burns found that claim credible. She relied on the accounts of city employees:

“City employees stated that [the former commissioner] was very aggressive with them in his pursuit of exceptions to existing codes or standards on behalf of developers. Employees also stated that Commissioner Rardin had been very aggressive with them in pursuit of exceptions to codes and standards on behalf of developers and other businesses. Employees reported that they feel that their jobs are in jeopardy when Commissioners directly interact with them and are critical of their performance.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

Burns found that this conduct broke the city's rules:

“The direct contact by commissioners with City employees in which commissioners attempt to influence how business is conducted violates the Code of Conduct, including the prohibition of engaging in executive management functions and prohibition against conduct that creates an appearance of impropriety. It also affects the public trust by creating a perception of misuse of public positions.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

The city's Code of Conduct, Ordinance 2-02-060, bars the commission from running city operations. In a December 2022 email included as an exhibit to the report, then-City Attorney Ashley Smith quoted subsection (q) to a commissioner:

“The Governing Body shall not perform general executive management functions in the administration of city government; these functions shall be delegated to the City Manager…” — Ordinance 2-02-060(q), as quoted by the City Attorney

The former commissioner, who was Mayor Pro Tem in 2023 and is no longer in public office, co-owns a local contracting business with his brother. He denied any financial interest in the subdivisions at issue, but acknowledged that his company does work for the city and local businesses and said he abstains from related votes. He told Burns he had discussed a developer's utilities and paving issue with the Public Works inspector and director, both of whom he felt were not being "business-friendly."

Pressure on the inspector and "substandard work"

Cesar alleged that the city's Public Works inspector and two directors were targeted by the former commissioner. Employee accounts supported the allegation:

“One employee indicated that [the former commissioner] pressured the approval of substandard work in a subdivision and the employee stopped dealing with [the former commissioner] because he was so combative.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

“Several commissioners interviewed confirmed that commissioners involved in the building industry have been openly critical of the Utilities and Public Works staff.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

The former commissioner denied any verbal abuse but said he had expressed frustration over code enforcement. Burns concluded:

“Mr. Cesar's allegation that elected officials have interfered with the management functions of the City and have attempted to influence how codes and ordinances should be applied is a credible allegation. This conduct by the elected officials identified in this allegation creates an appearance of impropriety and affects the public trust by creating a perception of misuse of public positions.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

The "cheater pipe"

Cesar alleged that after the Public Works inspector found a "cheater pipe" installed in a water meter by the former commissioner's company, the former commissioner contacted him about it. In his notarized statement, Cesar said the discovery followed standard procedure: Water Billing was notified, and they notified the Alamogordo Police Department. The report records the former commissioner's account:

“[The former commissioner] acknowledged that a “cheater pipe” was found and that he called the former City Attorney to let her know. He claimed that other contractors also used cheater pipes. … He also questioned whether the Utilities Director ever worked because his employees reported that the Director's truck was always at his house. The Utilities Director was aware that photos were taken of him by employees of [the former commissioner's company] while he was on leave.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

Burns found the allegation credible:

“Elected officials should not interfere with or attempt to influence code enforcement. Mr. Cesar's allegations of such interference and efforts to influence are credible.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

Commissioner by commissioner: the 2023 and 2025 findings

Burns did not sustain every allegation. The table below summarizes each official, the allegations against them, and her findings.

The 2023 report also addressed a sexual harassment allegation. A former city attorney reported in her exit interview that a commissioner alleged by other staff as being, Josh Rardin, had engaged in sexual harassment. The Burns report does not name the commissioner but multiple staff had collaborated it was a “well known unspoken secret it was Josh Rardin”. Burns found no violations by the then  mayor Susan Payne of any rules violations related to the handling of the harassment complaint and wrote that Cesar, as the city attorney's supervisor, "should have ensured that steps were taken to investigate it."

The report does not indicate that the allegation was ever investigated internally or in detail as a part of her inquiry.

In his notarized statement, Cesar wrote that the same commissioner later made remarks in front of the former city attorney and staff.

Burns summarized her 2023 findings this way:

“In summary, the allegations found to be credible involved conduct by Commission members in which they were directly interceding in day-to-day operations of the City and doing so with subordinate City staff members, placing those staff members in sometimes untenable positions.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

2025: "Credible evidence that the recruitment process has been tainted"

After Cesar's successor, Rick Holden, resigned on Sept. 19, 2024, due to health concerns but during a period of intense commissioner interference into his role as reported via Alamogordo Town News at the time. Dr. Stephanie Hernandez applied for the permanent job as an internal candidate. The 2025 investigation was opened over concerns that the search was biased against her. Burns set out the facts that shaped her analysis:

“She was the highest scorer in the interviews for the City Manager position and was the only passing score. She also is the only female candidate.” — Kemp Smith report, July 3, 2025

“There was corroborated evidence from witnesses that a commissioner (Rardin) made comments questioning Ms. Hernandez's qualifications and specifically suggesting she is not qualified for the position and will not receive that commissioner's vote, along with others.” — Kemp Smith report, July 3, 2025

Burns acknowledged that each commissioner may vote as they wish. She then warned of the legal risk:

“If a candidate is well-qualified, as the evidence supports that Ms. Hernandez is, and if she is the only candidate that passed the interview scoring, as she was, and she is the only female, as she was, but she is not selected, that allows for the argument that her non-selection is not legitimate but is discriminatory.” — Kemp Smith report, July 3, 2025

Witnesses named Rardin. Payne told the investigator she believed Rardin was biased against Hernandez and had pushed for the Sacramento Foundation to fund the search, which she believed was meant to intimidate Hernandez. McDonald gave the following account:

“Ms. (Redacted)  reported Commissioner's Rardin's comments to Mayor Pro Tem McDonald and she reported them to the City Attorney, as she felt his comments were inappropriate.” — Kemp Smith report, July 3, 2025

McDonald also told the investigator that some commissioners appeared to treat only male candidates as acceptable, and that the "type" certain commissioners wanted appeared to be a middle-aged white man. Other commissioners disagreed. Commissioner Tapley said he had heard no biased comments, and Commissioners Burnett and Robinson called Hernandez qualified. Robinson told the investigator it was well known that some on the commission did not support her candidacy, but that he was not among them.

Burns found no evidence that the process had been tilted in Hernandez's favor as an internal candidate in fact opposite, against her and “tainted.” She recommended starting over with a search firm hired by the city, not by the Sacramento Foundation, and concluded:

“In summary, my investigation found credible evidence that the recruitment process has been tainted.” — Kemp Smith report, July 3, 2025

Settlements and departures

The reports do not by themselves establish why each official left the city. But the departures that followed track closely with the conduct they describe:

April 2023: Cesar sends his letter. Instead of the scheduled evaluation, he negotiates a retirement and settlement agreement with the city.• 2023: Rick Holden is hired as city manager. He resigns on Sept. 19, 2024. The 2025 report does not state his reasons.

May 2025: The city cancels the recruitment that Burns found "tainted.”

March 10, 2026: The commission votes 7–0 to open contract negotiations with Hernandez

April 28, 2026: After closed sessions, the commission votes 4–3 to accept a settlement tied to an EEOC complaint Hernandez had filed. Rardin, Burnett, Al Hernandez and Baxter Pattillo vote in favor; Mayor McDonald and Commissioners Tapley and Robinson vote against.

On May 5, the commission votes 4-3 to approve final terms that include a 60-day separation

June 30, 2026: Hernandez's last day. The city attorney also resigns, leaving both top administrative posts vacant.

In her farewell remarks, Hernandez described a recurring pattern without naming anyone. "Going around the City Manager to directors has undermined the position," she said. She told the commission she had seen the practice under multiple city managers. This testimony confirms the legal investigations findings in a public forum. 

A pattern, and a commission that polices itself

Taken together, the two reports, the harassment claim described by staff, and a pending complaint against a sitting commissioner describe the same recurring problem: elected officials accused of pressuring or disparaging city employees, and a Code of Conduct process that rarely produces consequences.

The pending complaint. Item No. 10 on the Sept. 22 agenda, submitted by City Manager Robert Stockwell, asks the commission to decide whether a Code of Conduct complaint against Commissioner Al Hernandez goes forward. A three-member Preliminary Review Committee made up of fellow commissioners reviewed the four counts. Two members found "No Cause" on all four, and the third found "Cause" on all four. Because of the split, city code sends the question to the full commission. The motion needs five votes to pass, and Hernandez cannot vote. According to the agenda report, if the motion fails, "no further action on the complaint may be taken." The vote decides only whether the allegations will be examined, not whether they are true. 

The airport board video. The complaint comes as a clip from a public airport board meeting circulates online. In it, Commissioner Hernandez appears to call the leader of the city employees' union "stupid" and says she is causing problems for the city. A related public records request, No. 26-1438, is on file with the city. 

https://youtube.com/shorts/THi1Cm40-Rw?is=SvHAX3KDlzu_58e4

Outside counsel found problems; the commission did not. Both the 2023 and 2025 findings came from an outside attorney hired by the city, not from the commission's own review process. The 2023 report also shows how thin that process was. It said Code of Conduct complaints about workplace discrimination or harassment go to an ethics panel that had not yet been formed:

“The Code of Conduct provides that any complaint regarding workplace discrimination or harassment in violation of the Code of Conduct should be presented to the ethics panel (which is to be created under the Code of Conduct) by delivering a complaint to the City Attorney's office.” — Kemp Smith report, Dec. 22, 2023

On the former city attorney's harassment report, Burns found "no clear guidance from the Code of Conduct on how the complaint should be handled." The Code of Conduct itself, the report notes, prohibits elected officials from harassing anyone or retaliating against anyone who has complained of a violation.

Some commissioners resisted the code from the start. In his notarized statement, Cesar recounted that during the April 2023 executive session on his letter, Commissioner Melton said, "This is why I was against passing the Code of Conduct Ordinance." Cesar also wrote that Commissioner Rardin said, "If an investigation happens, Nancy needs to be investigated." Nancy Beshaler was the Public Works Director whom the 2023 report found commissioners had criticized directly. 

Two codes, no fix. Commissioners have identified two overlapping Code of Conduct ordinances, one from 2014 and one from 2022, with inconsistent language on complaint procedures and remedies. They asked staff to merge or repeal one, and the issue came up again in 2025. The 2023 report's recommendation of regular commission training on the limits of its role appears in the record only as a recommendation. In March of 2026, under acting City Manager, Dr Hernandez the commissioners held a public meeting in which OMA compliance and conduct training was held. During that session the commissioners in question to include Josh Rardin, Al Hernandez and Stephen Burnett seemed distracted, were on their cell phones looking or texting and were not deeply engaged in the presentation.

Critics point to three structural weaknesses in the current process and with the city charter. There is no independent investigator or hearing officer.

A five-vote supermajority lets a minority of commissioners end a complaint without any public review of the evidence.

And employees who are the subject of a commissioner's conduct have no formal role in the decision.

Supporters of the system counter that commissioners answer to voters, not staff, and that a high bar protects officials from politically motivated complaints. 

Residents can also take complaints outside City Hall, to the New Mexico Attorney General or the State Ethics Commission.

For employees, the stakes are the ones Burns described in 2023, when she found commissioners were placing city staff "in sometimes untenable positions."

Potential legal consequences under state and federal law

The conduct described in the reports touches several state and federal laws. What follows describes those laws in general terms. Whether any official or the city is liable would be decided by the agencies and courts that enforce them. 

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (federal). Title VII bars employers, including cities, from refusing to hire someone because of sex or national origin. It is enforced through complaints to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the process Hernandez used. Burns's warning that Hernandez's non-selection could be argued to be "discriminatory" describes this kind of claim. Title VII contains exceptions for certain policy-level appointees of elected officials, and how those exceptions apply to a city manager is a question for attorneys.

New Mexico Human Rights Act (NMSA 1978, § 28-1-7). The state law separately prohibits hiring discrimination based on sex, national origin and other protected traits. Complaints go through the state Human Rights Bureau, and remedies can include damages and attorney fees.

U.S. Constitution, Equal Protection Clause (42 U.S.C. § 1983). Government officials acting in their official roles can face federal civil-rights suits alleging intentional sex discrimination in public employment decisions.

New Mexico Whistleblower Protection Act (NMSA 1978, §§ 10-16C-1 to -6). Public employers may not retaliate against employees who report unlawful or improper conduct. Remedies include reinstatement, double back pay and attorney fees. The employees who told Burns they feared for their jobs, and Cesar's written complaint about commission conduct, are the kinds of reports the law protects.

New Mexico Public Employee Bargaining Act (NMSA 1978, § 10-7E-19). Public employers may not interfere with, restrain or coerce employees in exercising their collective bargaining rights, or discriminate against them for union activity. When an elected official publicly disparages a union leader in an official meeting, the legal exposure falls on the city, not on the official personally.

New Mexico Governmental Conduct Act (NMSA 1978, § 10-16-1 et seq.). The act requires public officers to treat their office as a public trust and to use their powers for the public interest, not private gain. It also restricts official acts that affect an officer's own financial interest. The 2023 report's findings about a then commissioner whose company did work in the city he helped govern raise questions this law is designed to address.

Commission-Manager Act (NMSA 1978, § 3-14-12) and the Open Meetings Act (NMSA 1978, § 10-15-1 et seq.). Citizen complaints filed with the State Ethics Commission and the Attorney General's Office cite these laws. They allege that commissioners directed staff around the city manager and made key personnel decisions in closed session.

Under the Open Meetings Act, an action not taken in compliance with the law is invalid. Cesar's notarized statement also recounts the assistant city manager warning commissioners in April 2023 about creating a "rolling quorum" over email. Rolling quorum concerns continue and are a component of the open meetings act litigation ongoing against the city in the Case Edwards v Alamogordo City Commission being litigated in the 12th Judicial Circuit. 

Inspection of Public Records Act (NMSA 1978, § 14-2-1 et seq.). Public records in New Mexico are presumed open to inspection. Agencies that wrongly withhold them can be ordered to pay damages and the requester's attorney fees. 

Beyond any penalties to individual officials, the cost falls on taxpayers. Settlements with departing managers, legal defense and repeated recruitment are paid from the city's budget at taxpayer expense.

item.title: Tularosa Trustees Weigh Dog Ordinance Rewrite, Hear Conditions for Proposed 190-Foot Cell Tower
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees took the first step toward rewriting the village's animal ordinance at its September regular meeting, while planning and zoning officials laid out a long list of conditions they say a proposed 190-foot cell tower on Sunset Road should have to meet before it could be built.

Trustees approved a notice of intent to adopt Ordinance No. 286, a major revision of the village code covering animals, enforcement, and dangerous and potentially dangerous dogs. Village attorney Nan Winter said the vote simply starts a two-step process. The draft will be published, a redline copy will be available from the village clerk, and the board will go through it line by line at its October 21 meeting.

Several trustees objected that the draft lists specific breeds as dangerous. One trustee said a dog's behavior depends on how its owner trains it, not its breed, and suggested the ordinance instead apply to dogs that have been reported and formally "deemed" dangerous. Other board members agreed. Winter said changes can be made at the October hearing without re-noticing the ordinance.

The proposal had already drawn public comment. Resident Michael Gruger warned against open-ended "grandfathering" for households that already have many animals and suggested a firm compliance date. The mayor responded that residents who currently exceed the proposed five-animal limit would need an inspection by the animal control officer before any exemption is granted.

Cell tower conditions

Planning and Zoning presented its findings of fact and recommended conditions for a special use permit sought by Flagship One LLC for a 190-foot self-supporting wireless tower at 44 Sunset Road. The commission took no position on whether the tower should be approved, and the board did not vote.

If trustees approve the permit, the commission recommends these conditions:

• The applicant must post a $75,000 removal bond, adjusted annually for inflation.

• The owner must certify each year that the tower remains in use. After 12 months of inactivity, the tower must be removed down to three feet below grade.

• Two antenna positions at or below 150 feet would be reserved for village and public safety equipment at nominal cost.

• The applicant must submit sealed engineering plans, a site-specific geotechnical report, an FCC radio-frequency emissions report, and historic and environmental clearances before a building permit is issued.

• Backup power would be limited to batteries. Adding a fuel-powered generator would require separate village approval.

• The access drive must be graveled to control dust.

The commission noted that federal "shot clock" rules require the village to issue a final decision within 150 days of receiving a complete application. Failing to do so could expose the village to a federal lawsuit. A public hearing, with newspaper notice and letters to nearby property owners, must still be scheduled. Commissioner Virgil "Bucky" Johnson was widely praised for his detailed questioning of the applicant.

During public comment, resident Larry Berry said he hoped the tower isn't built. He added that if one must be built, it should go on the 80 acres the village recently purchased, so the village collects the lease revenue.

Grants, fees and policy

The board approved three resolutions tied to infrastructure funding:

• Accepting a New Mexico Environment Department grant, which appeared to be $500,000, for water system improvements.

• Applying to waive the $17,000 local match on a $340,000 state award for planning and design of First Street, from Highway 70 to Darby Lane. The mayor credited Trustee Mark Garwood with pushing the project for two years.

• Applying to the Water Trust Board for planning and design funds for phase two of wastewater treatment plant improvements.

Trustees gave final approval to an ordinance that lets the village set permit fees by resolution. They then adopted a fee schedule: $100 for site location permits, $250 for manufactured or mobile home placement, $200 for commercial site layouts, and $150 for variance requests. Accessory structures under 200 square feet will still need a permit but will pay no fee.

The board also approved personnel policy changes that set police officers' schedules at 86 hours per two-week period, with overtime paid beyond that. Trustees also approved a two-lot split for Nancy Carr on Riata Road.

Dog park and cleanups

Grant coordinator Kendra presented a volunteer committee's preferred site for a dog park: the yard at the 606 Center recycling center off Highway 70. The committee chose it over sites near the splash pad and on Fifth Street. A $3,426.22 New Mexico Clean and Beautiful grant will pay for benches and trash cans, and the money must be spent by June 2027. Trustees raised concerns about parking, truck access to the recycling dumpsters, and dogs escaping near the highway. Neighbor Kathy said trash already blows from the site onto her property.

Planning and Zoning also proposed a street-by-street code enforcement program. Each month, one street would get a free roll-off dumpster, a courtesy walk-through, and then a final inspection before any citations. Police Chief Geraldine Martinez urged the board to involve Code Enforcement Officer Dean Lester in shaping the plan. Earlier in the meeting, Martinez presented Lester with a letter of commendation for finding an elderly man who had been missing nearly six hours on an August day with temperatures approaching 100 degrees.

Other business

• Water: Public works director Angel said the reservoir is about three-quarters full. Watering limits remain in place so storage tanks can be full before the pond is cleaned in the next six to eight weeks. Twenty to 30 randomly selected households will receive bottles for lead and copper testing.

• Communication: Village Clerk Rebecca Garcia said Village Hall renovations are complete. She is also exploring a text-alert system to reach residents without social media.

• Animal shelter: Martinez said the shelter holds about 21 dogs, including several from the Carolina Moreno property. That case is on hold pending court competency proceedings.

• Budget: One trustee said a budget line item is already 157 percent spent two months into the fiscal year. He asked that the finance director attend an upcoming special meeting on employee evaluations and raises.

• Christmas parade: The Kiwanis Club will again host the Christmas Light Parade on the first Saturday in December, themed "Let Freedom Glow" for America's 250th anniversary.
